title: Tumor architecture shapes polarized malignant states that predict outcome and treatment response in high-grade serous ovarian cancer

blocks.html: High-grade serous ovarian carcinoma (HGSC) is the most common subtype of ovarian cancer and remains the most lethal gynecological malignancy. Clinical management relies on surgical debulking and combination (platinum/taxane) chemotherapy, with maintenance PARP inhibitors for patients with homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) and frequent use of anti-VEGF antibody bevacizumab<sup class="cite" data-refs="1">1</sup>. Despite high initial response rates, recurrence of therapy-resistant disease is nearly universal<sup class="cite" data-refs="2">2</sup>. Bulk transcriptomic subtypes (C1/mesenchymal, C2/immunoreactive, C4/differentiated, C5/proliferative) were defined to stratify patients into biologically and therapeutically distinct groups<sup class="cite" data-refs="3,4">3,4</sup>. However, these subtypes have shown inconsistent survival associations across cohorts and often reflect sample composition rather than underlying biology<sup class="cite" data-refs="5,6,7">5–7</sup>. They have also not yet translated into tools for predicting treatment response. No molecular classifier reliably identifies patients who will relapse early after chemotherapy, and while bevacizumab prolongs progression-free survival (PFS) by only a few months in a subset of patients, it rarely improves overall survival (OS)<sup class="cite" data-refs="8">8</sup>. Beyond HRD, treatment decisions in HGSC remain largely unguided by tumor biology.

Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has resolved the HGSC tumor microenvironment (TME) in greater detail, characterizing immune phenotypes<sup class="cite" data-refs="9">9</sup>, stromal subtypes and their prognostic contributions<sup class="cite" data-refs="10">10</sup>, site-specific immune evasion driven by mutational processes<sup class="cite" data-refs="11">11</sup>, treatment-associated remodeling under chemotherapy and immunotherapy<sup class="cite" data-refs="12,13,14">12–14</sup>, and tumor–immune cell interactions across disease sites<sup class="cite" data-refs="15,16,17,18">15–18</sup>. These advances have come from focused characterization of the non-malignant components of the TME; however, the malignant epithelial subsets have been defined and annotated inconsistently, with no shared classification across cohorts<sup class="cite" data-refs="19,20">19,20</sup>. Given the extensive chromosomal rearrangements and paucity of recurrent somatic mutations in HGSC<sup class="cite" data-refs="3,4">3,4</sup>, HRD status remains the only molecular characteristic used to stratify the disease<sup class="cite" data-refs="3,4">3,4</sup>. No unified framework describes epithelial diversity in HGSC, explains how it arises within and across tumors, or reconciles the states defined in individual studies.

In HGSC, epithelial state has been linked to the surrounding tissue, but which environmental features pattern that state, and how consistently they act across tumors, remain unresolved. Vázquez-García et al. demonstrated that epithelial signaling programs vary independently of clonal identity within individual patients and recur across patients with different genotypes<sup class="cite" data-refs="11">11</sup>, suggesting that recurrent epithelial heterogeneity reflects environmentally programmed plasticity. Similar findings exist in other cancers: pancreatic cancer organoids collapse to a common state in culture irrespective of genotype and adopt distinct states under defined microenvironmental conditions<sup class="cite" data-refs="21">21</sup>; in glioblastoma, malignant states are spatially organized around microenvironmental features such as hypoxic gradients<sup class="cite" data-refs="22">22</sup>. HGSC tumors are structurally heterogeneous, exhibiting both solid and papillary growth patterns, as well as detached spheroids within peritoneal ascites, each defining a distinct microenvironment capable of shaping epithelial states. Resolving these recurring malignant states alongside the environmental features that pattern them would establish a unified framework for HGSC heterogeneity.

Here we examine how the local environment shapes epithelial state across HGSC. We integrated scRNA-seq data from 13 published studies into an atlas of approximately 2 million cells from 362 samples and generated targeted spatial transcriptomics of 8 whole tissues and tissue microarrays representing 378 patients. We identify a dominant axis of secretory epithelial polarization, from progenitor-like SecA to injury-associated SecB, that recurs across tumors and varies within genetic clones. In tumors, SecB polarization tracks with distance from vasculature, in hypoxic regions where HIF/NF-κB-driven survival and glycolysis replace mitogenic signaling. SecB cells are enriched in ascites. Lymphocytes are excluded from these regions, whereas macrophages adopt a hypoxic, glycolytic program that mirrors epithelial adaptation. These macrophages co-organize with SecB cells into an immune-protected niche poised for dissemination. The SecB state is largely lost in patient-derived organoids and only partially recovered by environmental inputs such as IFNγ, and it is incompletely recapitulated with in vivo models. Clinically, SecB polarization predicts worse survival after standard chemotherapy across independent cohorts, yet it identifies the patients who benefitted from bevacizumab in the ICON7 trial23. Together, these findings link HGSC tumor architecture to epithelial state, the immune niche, and treatment response.
Secretory epithelial cells adopt conserved polarized states in HGSC

To resolve the cellular landscape and transcriptional diversity of HGSC, we integrated scRNA-seq datasets from 13 independent studies (Figure 1a,b, Figure S1, S2, Table S1). This atlas comprises 1,980,703 cells from 158 patients across 362 tissue samples spanning 12 anatomic sites: primary tumors (adnexa), common metastatic sites (omentum, peritoneum, bowel), ascites, and rarer locations (lymph node, diaphragm, liver, upper quadrant, pelvic cavity, bladder, colon; Figure 1c, Figure S3). The atlas includes both treatment-naïve and post-treatment samples (Figure 1d, Figure S3). We adopted a hierarchical annotation scheme, identifying 13 broad cell type lineages that we further resolved into 51 discrete cell types and states (Figure 1e, Figure S4, Table S2, S3).

The integrated epithelial compartment (575,366 cells) included a small ciliated subset (6,678 cells, 1.2%) defined by canonical fallopian tube ciliated cell markers (FOXJ1, CAPS, RSPH1, TPPP3), with the remainder representing a dominant secretory population (PAX8, WFDC2; Figure 1f, Table S4). Within the secretory cell subset, markers associated with lineage-related differentiation were not uniformly expressed. To resolve coordinated transcriptional programs within the secretory compartment, we applied non-negative matrix factorization, which identified two programs that represent an axis of variation among malignant secretory cells (Figure S5, Table S5). Importantly, this axis represents the dominant coordinated transcriptional program across tumors (principal component (PC)1 in 54% of samples, PC1-3 in 82%; Figure 1g). One pole, we termed Secretory A (SecA), was enriched for developmental transcription factors and progenitor markers: MECOM, SOX17, FBXO21, PBX1, LGR5, LPAR3, and RCN2 (Figure 1h, Figure S6). The other pole, which we termed Secretory B (SecB) was enriched for keratins and mucosal differentiation genes: KRT17, LCN2, TACSTD2, KRT7, KRT19, SLPI, and PRSS22 (Figure 1i, Figure S6). This axis was independent of programs defining cell cycle, stress response, interferon, EMT, or metallothionein signatures (Figure 1j, Figure S5). To facilitate downstream comparisons, we partitioned cells along this axis into three groups: SecA, Intermediate, and SecB, based on their factor usage. These boundaries reflect divisions along a continuum rather than distinct cell identities (Figure 1k).

Having established the axis is independent of cell cycle and stress programs, we next asked whether it arises from genetic heterogeneity, leveraging inferred copy number variation (CNV) profiles. Within individual clones, we observed cells at both the SecA and SecB poles of the secretory axis (Figure 1l,m, Figure S7). This suggests that these states are not strictly driven by clonal divergence, though individual clones may differ in their propensity to activate specific programs.
SecB polarized cells represent a quiescent state, enriched in ascites

SecA and SecB cells exhibit distinct regulatory and metabolic features (Figure 2a). We characterized the transcriptional programs of SecA and SecB cells through gene set enrichment (Hallmark), and inferred pathway (PROGENy), transcription factor (DoRothEA) and metabolic activity (scFEA). SecA cells were enriched for proliferation and growth programs, including MAPK signaling (PROGENy); MYC and E2F targets (Hallmark, DoRothEA); and metabolic flux estimation consistent with biosynthetic growth (Figure 2a, Figure S8). In contrast, SecB cells were enriched for signals related to environmental adaptation, including hypoxia, p53, VEGF, and TGFβ, and were metabolically more glycolytic (Figure 2a). Cell cycle analysis confirmed this distinction: SecA cells had the highest proliferating fraction (37.8% S/G2M), whereas SecB cells were predominantly in G1 (80.6% G1, Figure 2b).

We quantified the proportion of each epithelial state across anatomic sites and after chemotherapy (Figure S9). Among pre-treatment samples, ascites was strongly enriched for SecB cells (68%), whereas primary and metastatic tumors showed similar SecB proportions (14% and 17%, respectively); this held in a subset of patient-matched multi-site samples (n = 14, median 60.7% in ascites vs 10.2% in primary; Figure 2c,d). In post-chemotherapy primary tumors, SecA proportions declined (from 60% to 53%) and SecB proportions increased (from 14% to 24%, Figure 2c). In a subset of patient-matched pre- and post-chemotherapy samples (n = 18), SecB increased after chemotherapy in 12 of the 18 patients (58% to 69%, p = 0.11, Figure 2e).

These findings suggest SecB cells may be dependent on the tumor microenvironment they exist within. We therefore asked if SecB cells are differentially enriched within the previously established molecular subtypes of HGSC tumors3,4. We categorized primary samples from the atlas into their TCGA-defined subtype using consensusOV, then explored the proportion of epithelial states within each (Figure 2f). We observed that SecA cells predominate in proliferative and immunoreactive tumors (median 76% and 75%) but were lower in differentiated and mesenchymal tumors (median 38% and 37%), while SecB was most abundant in mesenchymal tumors (Figure 2f). Together, these data suggest SecB polarization reflects a quiescent, metabolically adapted state that may confer an advantage under environmental stress, such as hypoxia and after exposure to chemotherapy. To explore secretory polarization across independent models and platforms, we derived a SecA/SecB gene signature from each NMF factor loading and used it to score polarization in downstream analyses, providing consistent, atlas-aligned thresholds (Figure 2g, Table S6).
In vitro and in vivo models of HGSC incompletely recapitulate secretory polarization

To assess whether we could model and perturb this secretory polarization in vitro, we performed snRNA-seq on eight patient-derived organoid (PDO) models derived from ascites (n = 4) or primary tumors (n = 4) (Figure 3a). Compared to the atlas, PDO models were strongly skewed toward SecA, with fewer than 1% of cells reaching the SecB signature threshold (Figure 3b). PDOs established from ascites samples, however, consistently exhibited higher SecB scores than those from primary tumors (p = 0.029), suggesting partial retention of this state from the ascites (Figure 3b).

Consistent with environmental maintenance of SecB, polarization scores in the OPTO98 PDO declined progressively over time in standard Matrigel-embedded, glucose-rich culture (Figure 3c). To attempt to identify the signals responsible, we treated organoids with candidate microenvironmental factors (IFNγ, TNFα, TGFβ, and WNT7A). Of all these perturbations, only IFNγ induced SecB gene expression across the population (Figure 3d), suggesting a role for the immune microenvironment in initiating or maintaining secretory polarization. We additionally tested if we could induce SecB polarization by differing culturing medias, but unfortunately no medium was able to recapitulate the SecB polarization observed in the atlas (Figure 3e).

We next asked whether the SecB state was represented across publicly available RNA-seq datasets of organoids and spheroids derived from HGSC (Figure 3f). We scored these models on their ability to recapitulate the SecB markers and function (HIF induction and quiescence) against the atlas reference (Figure 3f–h). While models cultured in hypoxic conditions recapitulate HIF induction (Figure 3g), proliferation rates remain elevated across models (Figure 3h). These data suggest that our current organoid and spheroid models lack the diverse cellular interactions and tissue-level features required to recapitulate the SecB state.

To explore the possibility of modeling SecB in vivo, we profiled the cellular composition of one primary endpoint tumor from the KPCA.B orthotopic syngeneic model of HGSC by scRNA-seq (Figure 3i). We identified several programs driving secretory cell heterogeneity within the KPCA.B model (Figure 3j, Figure S10), with expression of the top conserved SecB marker, KRT7, establishing a clear axis (Figure 3k). Immunohistochemistry on KPCA.B tumors, localized KRT7+ cells to luminal regions, where they appeared distant from the stroma and were frequently adjacent to immune cells (Figure 3l). Although the syngeneic model may be able to partially model a SecB-like state, no resulting NMF program reflected the human SecB polarization (Figure S10). The species-driven differences in epithelial and immune cell regulation and divergence from the disease’s natural progression by orthotopic cell injection may limit its ability to reflect the human SecB state.
Tumor architecture establishes a metabolic gradient aligned with secretory polarization

To identify the environmental features that drive the SecB state, we designed a custom targeted spatial transcriptomics panel (10x Genomics Xenium) to resolve cell types, epithelial programs, signaling pathways, immune function, therapeutic targets, and clinical classifiers relevant to HGSC (Table S7). We applied this panel to 8 whole HGSC tumors (n = 4 treatment-naïve, n = 4 post-chemotherapy, approximately 1.9 million cells, Table S8), to two tissue microarrays (TMAs) of primary HGSC representing a combined 378 patients (503 cores, 1.5 million cells: TMA A, 95 patients, 82 profiled in duplicate cores; TMA B, 283 patients), and to 15 healthy fallopian tube epithelial (FTE) tissue cores (34,281 cells, Figure 4a, Figure S11–13). Eighteen cell types, including ciliated and secretory epithelial cell states, were annotated by SingleR using the scRNA-seq atlas as a qualitative reference (Figure S14). Hierarchical clustering revealed broad diversity in HGSC tissue composition, with whole tissues spanning the range observed across the TMA patients (Figure 4a). Secretory cells were scored for polarization (SecB – SecA) and annotated according to atlas-aligned thresholds, with polarization scoring significantly higher in the HGSC secretory cells compared to those within the healthy FTE tissue (per-unit medians, p = 0.003, Figure S15).

Across all eight whole tissues, SecA and SecB scores were spatially segregated (Figure 4b,c): a cell's SecA score was negatively associated with its neighbors' SecB scores within each whole tissue (bivariate Moran's I −0.01 to −0.17; sign test p = 0.008) and in 299 of 334 TMA patients (Wilcoxon p < 0.001), forming continuous spatial polarization gradient toward the lumen of papillary growths (Figure 4d). Whereas SecA cells were broadly distributed throughout HGSC tissue, SecB cells were spatially concentrated: 89% of SecB cells assigned to a neighborhood resided in neighborhoods enriched for other SecB cells, suggesting that this adaptation occurs in discrete, spatially coherent niches (Figure 4e). To understand what shapes these niches, we characterized the local microenvironment (50 µm radius) of each secretory cell (1,235,350 cells) and quantified regional cell type composition, bulk environmental signaling, and cell-specific gene expression. We used generalized additive modeling to map local environmental changes along the polarization axis (pathway UCell scores using custom gene sets, Table S9). In the tissue maps, SecB cells lay toward the lumen of papillary structures (Figure 4b,c), and they were enriched with increasing distance from the vasculature (Figure 4f–h, Figure S16). These shifts coincide with reduced local cell density (Figure 4f,i) and increased expression of matrix remodeling genes (e.g. ADAM17, MMP7, SERPINE1, Figure 4f). These architectural and compositional changes are associated with shaping the local metabolic environment; as secretory cells move away from blood vessels, expression of hypoxia-associated genes (e.g. ENO1, HIF1A, VEGFA) increased (Figure 4f,j).
SecB cells and macrophages adapt to hypoxic niches through a shared glycolytic survival program

We next examined how transcriptional programs within the secretory cells adapt along the secretory polarization axis (Figure 5a–d). Within secretory epithelial cells, we observed a consistent decline across markers of proliferation and growth as cells adapt toward SecB, including: proliferation signals (MKI67, PCNA, TOP2A), oncogenic growth signaling pathways (Myc [MYC, MAX, MYCL], PI3K [PIK3CA, AKT1, MTOR], Wnt [FZD3, CTNNB1, TCF7L2], and Notch [JAG1, NOTCH1, NOTCH2]), DNA damage repair genes (BRCA1/2, ATM, CHEK2), and epigenetic remodeling signals (DNMT3A, HDAC1, KDM5A) (Figure 5a,c,d; Figure S17). Instead, SecB cells maintain survival through increased TNFA expression, NF-κB signaling (BIRC3, ICAM1, NFKBIA), and HIF-driven glycolysis (SLC2A1, LDHA, SLC16A3; Figure 5a,c,d). Consistent with reduced proliferation and growth signaling, SecB cells had significantly smaller nuclei than SecA cells across our Xenium tissues (median 39.5 vs 47.7 µm², p = 0.008) and across the TMA cohort (n = 361 patients, p < 0.001; Figure 5b). These signals suggest that SecB cells adapt to their hypoxic environment by trading proliferation for stress-tolerant survival.

The hypoxic niches that enriched for SecB cells also showed coordinated shifts in immune composition. By modeling the composition of each cell's neighborhood as a function of local epithelial hypoxia across the eight whole tissues, we found that macrophages and B cells followed opposite trajectories: macrophages rose from 13.4% to 32.6% of non-epithelial cells in the most hypoxic niches, whereas B cells fell from 3.8% to 0.7% (both p = 0.008, 8 of 8 tissues; Figure 5e–h). Within hypoxic regions, T cells and plasma cells trended lower, and NK cells were unchanged (Figure 5e-h). Macrophages not only persisted in the most metabolically stressed niches but activated a transcriptional program mirroring the SecB survival program (Figure 5i,j; Figure S18). Macrophages in SecB regions adopted glycolytic (LDHA, ENO1, PGK1, ALDOA) and NF-κB (ICAM1, NFKBIA, BIRC3) programs with reduced tissue-resident identity (A2M, C1QC, Figure 5i). They concurrently maintained chemokine production (CXCL10, CXCL11), signaling for lymphocyte recruitment into the metabolically hostile niche (Figure 5i). This transcriptional program also aligned with a coordinated morphological shift, with SecB-adjacent macrophages being larger than SecA-adjacent macrophages (Figure 5j).
SecB epithelium co-opts a hypoxic macrophage state into a self-sustaining pro-dissemination niche

To better describe the relationship between macrophages and SecB cells sequestered within the niche, we performed Visium HD on one of our Xenium tissues (WT01, Figure 4). This sample was selected as it held the highest proportion of SecB (Figure 4a, Figure 6a Table S8). By Visium HD, we were able to further confirm that the spatially driven SecB polarization aligns with transcriptional expression of the hypoxia-associated CA9 (Figure 6b–d). We compared the macrophage bins adjacent to SecB-high epithelium to distal macrophage bins and found that SecB macrophages upregulate expression of osteopontin (SPP1) (Figure 6e) and MMP9, among other known hypoxia response genes (Table S10). This transcriptional program aligned to the hypoxic macrophages within the atlas (Figure 6f) and reflected the glycolytic program we described (Figure 5i). Across our Xenium tissues, macrophages defined by this hypoxic program had twice the proportion of SecB neighbors among their epithelial neighbors compared to resident-like macrophages (Figure 6g).

Within this niche, SecB cells and hypoxic macrophages exchange survival and immune-protective signals. We explored differentially expressed genes from SecB-niche versus control macrophages across our datasets, and within our Xenium we also looked at SecB cells directly in contact with (within 30µm of) adjacent a SecB-niche macrophages. Macrophages express VEGFA, while SecB cells in contact with them further upregulate their downstream NF-κB target BIRC3 potentially amplifying their survival program (Figure 6h,i). SecB cells in turn protect themselves from macrophage phagocytosis and complement by upregulating CD47 and CD55, respectively (Figure 6h,i). Additionally, we observed that SecB cells could be engaging in direct immunosuppression through the upregulation of IL-32 and galectin-9 (LGALS9), with galectin-9 further increasing upon macrophage contact (Figure 6h,i). Notably, SecB cells upregulate SLC16A3 (MCT-4), which likely contributes to the lymphocyte-hostile environment by acidifying the niche (Figure 6h,i).

This niche also contains a coordinated adhesion and matrix-remodeling program that could favor dissemination. SPP1 receptor, CD44, was also found enriched on macrophages within the niche (Figure 6h,i). Additionally, SecB cells upregulated ICAM1, especially upon macrophage contact, which could provide SecB cells with a tether to immune or mesothelial cells (Figure 6h,i). These SecB cells and macrophages within this niche also likely collaborate to constantly remodel this environment. For example, SecB cells express MMP7 and TIMP1, alongside macrophages that produce enzymes, including cathepsins such as CTSL, which can accelerate remodeling (Figure 6h,i). Both cells contribute to TGM2 expression supporting local remodeling (Figure 6h). Together, these signals likely support homotypic and heterotypic adhesions within a niche marked by extracellular matrix remodeling (Figure 6h,i).
Secretory polarization independently predicts survival and bevacizumab response

To assess the impact of secretory polarization on clinical outcomes, we performed survival analyses in patients represented by two primary, treatment-naive HGSC cores (OS n = 104, PFS n = 103). Patients in the highest polarization tertile (SecB-enriched) had worse 5-year OS than those in the lowest tertile (SecA-dominant; p = 0.011), and a trend towards worse 5-year PFS (p = 0.11; Figure 7a,b). In multivariable Cox regression adjusted for stage, residual disease and age, SecA proportion was protective for OS (HR = 0.68 per SD, 95% CI 0.51–0.90, q = 0.029) and PFS (HR = 0.79, 95% CI 0.63–0.98, q = 0.048), whereas SecB proportion was associated with worse OS (HR = 1.38, 95% CI 1.06–1.78, q = 0.030), with a similar trend for PFS (HR = 1.23, 95% CI 1.00–1.50, q = 0.051; Figure 7c,d). Consistent with this, the continuous per-patient polarization score (mean cell-level polarization across all secretory cells) was independently prognostic for OS (HR = 1.51, 95% CI 1.11–2.07, q = 0.029), with a similar trend for PFS (HR = 1.27, 95% CI 0.999–1.62, q = 0.051), indicating that the secretory polarization state, not just the abundance of either pole, carries clinical relevance (Figure 7c,d; Table S11).

We next correlated our Xenium transcript counts and polarization scores with the abundance of prognostic proteins previously measured on a subset of the same cores. We found that transcript counts and protein abundance were strongly correlated for SecB markers KRT7 and KRT19 (KRT7: Pearson r = 0.64; KRT19: Pearson r = 0.63; Figure 7e). Furthermore, mean polarization scores also correlated with protein abundance for these two SecB markers, while E-cadherin, VIM, and KRT18 showed no association with polarization score (Figure 7f). These results validate and contextualise earlier findings on this cohort demonstrating that KRT7 and KRT19 were independently associated with worse OS and PFS after correction for stage and residual disease24.

To validate these survival effects in an external cohort, we applied SecA-specific and SecB-specific gene signatures to bulk RNA-seq data from 314 TCGA-OV tumors, quantifying polarization as the difference between the z-scored SecB and SecA signatures4. Patients in the highest polarization tertile, SecB tumours, had significantly worse 5-year OS (p = 0.010) and PFS (p = 0.010) than those in the lowest tertile (Figure 7g,h). Cox proportional hazards regression confirmed that increased polarization was associated with worse OS (HR = 2.00, 95% CI 1.25–3.20, p = 0.004) and PFS (HR = 1.79, 95% CI 1.15–2.78, p = 0.009; Figure 7i,j). This association remained significant after adjustment for epithelial cell fraction, stage and age (OS HR = 1.84, 95% CI 1.10–3.07, p = 0.021; PFS HR = 1.65, 95% CI 1.03–2.64, p = 0.038; Figure 7i,j).

Given that SecB niches are relatively avascular (Figure 4g,h), we next asked whether the degree of SecB polarization could influence response to the anti-VEGF antibody bevacizumab, which is routinely used to treat HGSC. To test this, we scored secretory polarization in pre-treatment samples from stage III/IV patients enrolled in the ICON7 trial (n = 191), and we classified them as SecA-polarized (n = 96) or SecB-polarized (n = 95)23. Within each group, we compared outcomes between patients treated with carboplatin and paclitaxel alone or in combination with bevacizumab. Consistent with our previous analyses, each 1 SD increase in polarization predicted worse OS under standard chemotherapy (n = 95; HR 1.38, 95% CI 1.02–1.86, p = 0.038; Table S12). Importantly, prolonged PFS with bevacizumab was observed only in SecB-polarized tumors (HR 0.36, 95% CI 0.22–0.59, p < 0.001; median PFS 11.1 vs 18.7 months), with no benefit provided to SecA-polarized tumors (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.48–1.35, p = 0.41; median PFS 17.9 vs 21.6 months, Figure 7k,l). The treatment and polarization interaction was significant for PFS (median split HR 0.44, 95% CI 0.22–0.90, likelihood-ratio p = 0.025). In a time-varying analysis, the benefit in SecB tumors was specific to the first 15 months, during which bevacizumab was administered (HR 0.23, 95% CI 0.12–0.44, p < 0.001) but lost thereafter (HR 0.87, p = 0.77; period interaction p = 0.022; Figure 7m), whereas SecA tumors showed no period-specific effect (interaction p = 0.19; Figure 7n). Together these data suggest that the avascular niches of SecB tumors may make them more reliant on angiogenic signaling, and identify secretory polarization as a candidate biomarker associated with greater bevacizumab benefit, to be tested in prospective cohorts.

Here we show that tumor architecture is a dominant driver of epithelial heterogeneity in HGSC. Secretory epithelial cells span a polarization axis from proliferating, progenitor-like SecA to quiescent, environmentally adapted SecB. This polarization is driven by distance from vasculature and hypoxia rather than by clonal genotype. SecB cells co-organize with reprogrammed macrophages into immune-protected niches primed for dissemination. SecB-enriched tumors have worse outcomes after standard chemotherapy, yet preferentially benefit from bevacizumab, positioning secretory polarization as both a prognostic and a candidate predictive biomarker.

HGSC is characterized by extensive copy number alterations that could produce idiosyncratic, patient-specific phenotypes<sup class="cite" data-refs="25">25</sup>. Instead, we find secretory polarization broadly reproducible across patient samples: 93.5% of patients with ≥ 100 epithelial cells contain SecA, Intermediate, and SecB cells, all existing within individual clones. The proportion of each state varies by environment, with higher SecB representation in the ascites and in hypoxic microenvironments within solid tissue. Previous findings in glioblastoma have similarly demonstrated that recurrent malignant programs are shaped by hypoxic gradients rather than genotype<sup class="cite" data-refs="22,26">22,26</sup>.

However, SecA and SecB do not represent a generic pan-cancer program<sup class="cite" data-refs="27,28,29">27–29</sup>, the previously described therapy-associated stress signature (AP-1/IEG), nor EMT features (SNAI1/2, VIM)<sup class="cite" data-refs="15">15</sup>. Instead, they recapitulate the secretory lineage of the normal and injured fallopian tube epithelium. SecA cells express the canonical regulatory program of secretory progenitors, including MECOM, SOX17, FBXO21, PBX1, and LGR5<sup class="cite" data-refs="30,31">30,31</sup>. SecB cells reflect the keratin and alarmin program of injured mucosal epithelium, marked by KRT7/17/19<sup class="cite" data-refs="32">32</sup>, LCN2<sup class="cite" data-refs="33">33</sup>, SLPI<sup class="cite" data-refs="34">34</sup>, and TACSTD2/TROP2<sup class="cite" data-refs="35">35</sup>. Consistent with the developmental constraint model of cancer, these findings suggest that the microenvironment selects from states bound to its tissue of origin<sup class="cite" data-refs="36">36</sup>.

While the secretory polarization axis had not yet been identified, multiple SecB markers have been implicated in HGSC previously. KRT7<sup class="cite" data-refs="24,37,38">24,37,38</sup>, KRT17<sup class="cite" data-refs="39,40">39,40</sup>, KRT19<sup class="cite" data-refs="24,41,42">24,41,42</sup> and its cleaved fragment CYFRA21-1<sup class="cite" data-refs="43,44">43,44</sup>, and TROP2<sup class="cite" data-refs="37,45,46">37,45,46</sup> have been linked to poorer outcomes across HGSC cohorts. Additionally, within HGSC tumors, a spatial program termed differentiated-invasive, marked by elevated LCN2 and TACSTD2, was recently characterized and associated with poorer prognosis<sup class="cite" data-refs="47">47</sup>. Conversely, SecA-polarized regions likely reflect the spatial domains with high MHC-II expression, elevated antigen presentation (HLA-I and CIITA expression) and increased immune infiltration that have been previously identified as protective in HGSC patients<sup class="cite" data-refs="48,49,50">48–50</sup>. Additionally, secretory polarization may provide a cellular explanation for the link previously made between HGSC molecular subtypes and morphology-based architectural patterns<sup class="cite" data-refs="51">51</sup>. SecA cells were highly represented in the proliferative and immunoreactive tumors, while SecB cells were abundant in mesenchymal and differentiated subtypes.

SecB-polarized epithelial cells and macrophages assemble into a coherent niche at the luminal interface of papillary growth. Within this hypoxic niche, SecB cells trade proliferation for HIF/NF-κB-driven survival and glycolysis, upregulating MCT-4 (SLC16A3), which could acidify the niche and further contribute to lymphocyte exclusion52,53. Exclusion was most pronounced for B cells, which are generally associated with tertiary lymphoid structures and with favorable outcomes in HGSC54. B cell loss may therefore contribute to the poor prognosis of SecB-enriched tumors. Macrophages were instead retained while adopting a hypoxic, SPP1⁺ MMP9⁺ glycolytic state matching that of the tumor-associated macrophages previously linked to poor outcome across cancers, including HGSC55.

SecB cells and hypoxic macrophages appear to engage in reciprocal signaling that sustains the niche. Macrophages supply VEGFA, and SecB cells in contact with macrophages further activate NF-κB targets BIRC3 and ICAM1. SecB cells may in turn evade phagocytosis and complement recognition through CD47 and CD55, and may suppress immunity through galectin-9 and IL-32. These cells likely also coordinate adhesion and proteolysis programs within the niche. SecB-adjacent macrophages express cathepsins which can activate local matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs). Notably, CTSL, a marker of SecB adjacent macrophages, can promote matrix remodeling by inhibiting SecB expressed SLPI, which normally functions to protect against injury56. SPP1 expressing macrophages can engage CD44 on macrophages and SecB cells and these adhesion molecules in conjunction with elevated ICAM1 likely support multi-cellular anchorage within the niche57,58. Together, these programs likely support the establishment of cohesive, multicellular units that detach into ascites59,60. As ascites is a hypoxic fluid61 and is itself strongly enriched for SecB cells (68% vs 14% in primary tumors), these data support a model in which SecB niches provide a pre-adapted source of disseminating spheroids.

This SecB niche is quiescent and self-sustaining, and therefore may be expected to resist chemotherapy. Indeed, secretory polarization may provide a cellular explanation for why HGSC is often highly sensitive to initial chemotherapy, but recurs almost universally. The high proliferative fraction of SecA cells may render them particularly sensitive to platinum and taxane chemotherapy, contributing to this initial response. Conversely, SecB cells are predominantly in G1 and reside in poorly perfused regions that may limit drug delivery, which could favor persistence. Consistent with this, SecB proportions increased in post-chemotherapy primary tumors and rose after treatment in 12 of 18 patient-matched samples across various tumor sites. SecB-enriched tumors also had shorter survival across three independent cohorts. SecB cells may therefore represent a reservoir of drug-tolerant persisters that seed recurrence, a hypothesis testable by longitudinal sampling.

Secretory polarization may also explain the longstanding asymmetry in HGSC response to bevacizumab, which improves PFS in unselected patients but rarely OS. In ICON7<sup class="cite" data-refs="23">23</sup>, the PFS benefit of bevacizumab was confined to SecB-polarized tumors (HR 0.36; median 11.1 vs 18.7 months), with no significant benefit in SecA-polarized tumors, and was confined to the first 15 months, spanning treatment. SecB niches are poorly perfused and hypoxic yet enriched with macrophage-derived VEGFA, suggesting that they depend on ongoing angiogenic signaling. Anti-VEGF therapy may therefore suppress SecB niches only while administered, allowing them to re-emerge after withdrawal and accounting for PFS gains that do not translate into OS. Unlike prior candidate biomarkers for bevacizumab response, secretory polarization proposes a multi-cellular mechanism linked to clinical response, and therefore the degree of polarization could guide patient selection, maintenance duration, and inform combination therapies.

The fact that this state was not characterized previously can likely be attributed to the experimental models currently used to study HGSC. SecB was largely lost in our PDOs, which collapsed toward SecA, mirroring the previously reported collapse of basal and classical pancreatic cancer organoids into a default classical-like state<sup class="cite" data-refs="21">21</sup>. Likewise, neither published HGSC organoid or spheroid models, including those cultured under hypoxic conditions, nor the KPCA.B syngeneic model could recapitulate both the hypoxic and quiescent features of SecB. Furthermore, no environmental signal or culturing media composition tested was able to polarize cells to SecB within our PDOs, and only IFN-γ induced any meaningful SecB gene expression. This partial success with IFN-γ suggests that immune-derived signals may play a role in initiating polarization early in niche formation, prior to the establishment of the lymphocyte-excluding acidic and hypoxic cores. Altogether, these results suggest current preclinical platforms may be systematically biased toward the proliferative, chemo-sensitive SecA state, and screening these would underrepresent the population most likely to persist after chemotherapy. New models incorporating hypoxic gradients, immune signals and multicellular organization will be required to effectively study and target the SecB niche.

While we currently lack the complex systems required to model SecB, secretory polarization is already measurable with tools used in pathology. For example, KRT7 and KRT19 protein abundance tracked Xenium-defined polarization in the same TMA cores, whereas non-SecB epithelial markers (E-cadherin, KRT18, VIM) did not. This is consistent with prior reports that KRT7 and KRT19 independently predict worse survival<sup class="cite" data-refs="24">24</sup>. Beyond tissue, serum CYFRA 21-1, a cleaved KRT19 fragment, may offer a minimally invasive readout of SecB burden<sup class="cite" data-refs="43">43</sup>. There are therefore multiple potential strategies for testing polarization-based stratification prospectively without single-cell or spatial profiling. Prospective validation of these strategies against chemotherapy and bevacizumab outcomes will be required to translate these hypotheses to clinical application.

This study has several limitations that warrant future validation. The spatial analyses are observational and cannot establish whether tissue architecture induces, selects, or maintains secretory states. Hypoxia, metabolic activity, and signaling were inferred primarily from transcriptional expression rather than measured directly. Finally, clinical associations were examined retrospectively and the utility for treatment selection requires formal prospective validation.

Together, our findings position tissue organization as a dominant driver of epithelial heterogeneity in HGSC, shaping malignant cell states constrained by the developmental history of the cancer. These malignant states reciprocally interact with the TME, forming heterogeneous niches that emerge as recurrent units throughout the tumor and may drive distinct aspects of disease biology. Current cytotoxic therapy preferentially targets the proliferative SecA compartment, whereas the transient benefit of bevacizumab in SecB-polarized tumors suggests that the SecB niche is targetable by anti-VEGF therapy. Durable improvement of HGSC outcomes will likely require biomarker-guided use of existing agents combined with approaches that directly engage the SecB niche. Finally, disrupting the signaling that sustains the niche, as bevacizumab likely does, may prevent its persistence altogether.

Additional sheets list the scoring method for each dataset and the 177 SecA-specific and 177 SecB-specific genes used to score TCGA-OV.

Genes with ≥3 QC flags failed (31 genes). Of these, 28 were excluded from SingleR annotation (429 genes used for annotation), and three essential markers were retained with flags. All genes were retained for expression and pathway analyses; 20 genes absent from the atlas are marked Xenium-only.

The log2 fold change of mean CP10k is given before and after adjustment for macrophage content (median log2 fold change of pan-macrophage genes subtracted). Each gene is classified as macrophage-attributable, SecB epithelial carry-over or stromal, and bin-level Mann–Whitney p values with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR are reported descriptively. Xenium SecB-niche macrophages (≥5 SecB epithelial cells within 50 µm) were compared with control macrophages (no SecB and ≥5 SecA cells within 50 µm) by pseudobulk limma-voom paired by section, across 7 whole tissues with ≥50 macrophages per group (WT07 had 39 SecB-macrophages and was excluded). The Kaplan–Meier comparison of the lowest and highest polarization tertiles in Figure 7a,b (tertile cut-offs, group sizes, events, 5-year survival and log-rank p) is included.

tables.title: Cox regression of secretory polarization and bevacizumab benefit in the ICON7 trial
tables.html: Pre-treatment tumors from FIGO stage III/IV patients (GSE140082; n = 191) were classified as SecA-polarized (n = 96) or SecB-polarized (n = 95) at the cohort median polarization score. Every model is adjusted for FIGO stage, debulking status and age. The table reports the association of continuous polarization (per 1 SD) with OS and PFS within each treatment arm; the effect of bevacizumab on PFS within each polarization group (Figure 7k,l); the time-varying bevacizumab effect before and after 15 months, with the period interaction (Figure 7m,n); and the treatment x polarization-group interaction for PFS, with its likelihood-ratio test. Kaplan–Meier median survival, group sizes and all model coefficients are included. Benjamini–Hochberg q values for Figure 7m,n and for the period interaction are included.

methods.title: Experimental Model and Study Participant Details

blocks.html: Human Tissues. De-identified archival tissues were used under REBs #20240175-01H and #20240096-01H, with informed consent. We profiled three sources of tissues: eight FFPE HGSC whole tissues (WT01 – WT08), TMA A (101 patients, CHUM cohort) and TMA B (317 patients profiled, COEUR cohort) (Table S8).

Patient-derived organoids (PDOs). Eight HGSC organoids were used: OPTO98, OPTO112, OPTO129, and PDO66 from primary tumors and OCAD93, OCAD96, OCAD97 and OCAD106 from ascites. These were obtained from Princess Margaret Cancer Centre and Western University. Organoids were embedded in Matrigel (20,000–50,000 cells per 50 µL dome). The culture medium was Advanced DMEM/F-12 containing GlutaMAX (2 mM), HEPES (10 mM), antibiotic-antimycotic (100 U/mL), B27 (1×), N-acetyl-L-cysteine (1.25 mM), EGF (20 ng/mL), bFGF (100 ng/mL), FGF-10 (100 ng/mL), Noggin (100 ng/mL), nicotinamide (1 mM), Y-27632 (10 µM), forskolin (10 µM) and β-estradiol (200 nM). The PDO66 medium was further supplemented with N2 (1×), SB431542 (0.5 µM) and BMP2 (10 ng/mL). Organoids were passaged every 1–4 weeks after TrypLE dissociation.

Mice. KPCA.B cells were kindly provided by Dr. Robert Weinberg<sup class="cite" data-refs="62">62</sup> and 150,000 cells were implanted orthotopically into the ovarian bursa of C57BL/6 mice under protocol OHRIe-3632. Tumors were collected for scRNA-seq at day 34.

Single-cell atlas construction. We integrated raw counts from 13 published HGSC scRNA-seq studies (Table S1) on 14,470 shared genes. Cells with < 500 UMIs, or <300 genes were removed, as were Scrublet-called doublets63, and artifact clusters. Samples with fewer than 500 remaining cells were removed. The atlas retained 1,980,703 cells from 362 samples of 158 patients. Data were integrated using scVI and scANVI64 (batch set per sample), seeded with CellAssign65 labels as scANVI annotations. Leiden clusters were annotated (Figure S1-4, Table S2 – 4).

Copy number. CopyKAT66 was run per sample, with a minimum of 200 epithelial cells and 50 reference cells. Fibroblast, T/NK, and endothelial cells were used as the diploid reference. Subclones (with 20 or more cells) were defined by hierarchical clustering and silhouette width.

Epithelial NMF and states. NMF (sckit-learn, k = 10) was fitted on a stratified set of 50,000 secretory cells and then applied to all 575,366 epithelial cells. The factor 2 (SecB) usage was used to classify secretory cells as SecA (<50th percentile), Intermediate, or SecB (≥ 75th percentile). In 250 samples with a minimum of 150 aneuploid epithelial cells, we recorded the principal component of malignant expression most correlated with SecB-SecA score as the dominant secretory axis of polarization.

Functional inference of epithelial states. PROGENy67 and DoRothEA68 activities (decoupler, multivariate linear model), Hallmark scores and scFEA69 flux (human M168 model) were averaged per epithelial state. Cell-cycle phase was assigned with scanpy. ConsensusOV70 subtypes were assigned to whole-sample pseudobulks of pre-treatment, primary samples (n = 96 samples, 77 patients). SecB vs SecA differential expression was tested with PyDESeq2 (design ~sample + state, Wald test, BH) on sample-by-state pseudobulks (n = 261 samples, 135 patients).

Polarization scoring. Unless stated otherwise, polarization was the SecB – SecA UCell71 score on raw counts. SecA genes were MECOM, FBXO21, LGR5, LPAR3, PBX1, SOX17, and RCN2; SecB genes were KRT17, KRT19, KRT7, LCN2, PRSS22, SLPI and TACSTD2. They were selected for factor specificity, differential expression and cross-platform detectability. Each platform was scored in the gene space it shares with the atlas by UCell (Xenium, 457 genes; organoids, 14,271).TCGA-OV tumors were scored as the mean z-score of the 177 SecB -177 SecA NMF-specific genes. All gene sets are listed in Table S6 and Table S9. Visium HD bins were scored as the mean z-score of the SecB minus the SecA genes, and ICON7 arrays with UCell, each score z-scored across the 380 arrays. Organoid panels show the SecB UCell score.
Organoid snRNA-seq panel. PDOs were fixed and profiled with Parse Evercode WT v3. After doublet removal (scDblFinder) and QC (>500 UMIs, >300 genes, <20% mitochondrial reads), 10,455 cells remained.

Organoid experimental perturbations. OPTO98 organoids were cultured for 2,6,10 or 12 days of standard culture, with various environmental cytokines (IFNγ (20 ng/mL), TNFα (10 ng/mL), TGFβ (5 ng/mL), or WNT7A (500 ng/mL)), or eight varying medias (Basal media (BM, Advanced DMEM/F12, HEPES 10mM, antibiotic antimycotic 1X, B-27 supplement 1X, GlutaMax 1X, N-Acetyl-Cysteine 1mM), BM01 (BM + SB202190 0.5µM, A83-01 0.5µM, FGF-10 10ng/mL), BM02 (BM + FGF-4 10ng/mL), BM03 (BM + β-estradiol​ 100nM), BM1 (BM + Nicotinamide 5mM), BM2 (BM + EGF 5ng/mL, Heregulin-β-1 37.5ng/mL, hydrocortisone 0.5µg/mL, Forskolin 5µM), CGM (Advanced DMEM/F12, HEPES 10mM, antibiotic antimycotic 1X, B-27 supplement 1X, GlutaMax 1X, N-Acetyl-Cysteine 1.25mM, EGF 20ng/mL, β-FGF 100ng/mL, FGF-10 100ng/mL, Noggin 100ng/mL, Nicotinamide 1mM, Forskolin 10µM, β-estradiol​ 100nM, Y-27632 10µM), CGM Asc (CGM + cell free ascites fluid, 1:1) or HPLM (HPLM, HEPES 10mM, antibiotic antimycotic 1X, B-27 supplement 1X, GlutaMax 1X, N-Acetyl-Cysteine 1.25mM, EGF 20ng/mL, β-FGF 100ng/mL, FGF-10 100ng/mL, Noggin 100ng/mL, Nicotinamide 1mM, Forskolin 10µM, β-estradiol​ 100nM, Y-27632 10µM) for 6 days, with media replenished (in condition) every 3 days. At time of collection, organoids were subsequently dissociated using TrypLE for 45 min at 37°C and quenched with AdDMEM/F12. MULTI-seq barcoding, lipid-modified oligonucleotide anchor and barcode strands were prepared at a 1:1 molar ratio in serum-free PBS to generate sample-specific barcodes (2 µM, 10X anchor:barcode solution), alongside a 10X co-anchor solution (2 µM). Briefly, 50,000 cells per condition were washed twice and resuspended in 180 µL with PBS. Cells were incubated with 20 µL sample-specific 10X anchor: barcode solution on ice for 10 min with intermittent mixing every 3 min. This was followed by the addition of 22 µL of the 10X co-anchor solution and a further 10 min incubation with mixing occurring every 3 min on ice. Labeling was quenched with ice-cold 1% BSA-PBS, followed by two washes, filtration through a 40 µm strainer, and cell counting prior to downstream library preparation. These conditions were sample multiplexed in one 10X genomics library; after removing 4,017 doublets and 43 unassigned cells, 11,543 cells remained.

Organoid polarization quantification. We combined PDOs, atlas pseudobulk and three external datasets: DepMap organoids72, GSE29920073 and GSE28450774. All profiles were scored in one shared UCell space, with function defined as z(HIF) – z(proliferation). HIF: NDRG1, SLC16A3, VEGFA, CA9, BNIP3, P4HA1, PDK1, SLC2A1; Proliferation: MKI67, TOP2A, PCNA, CCNB1, CDK1.

KPCA.B tumor and Immunohistochemistry. One KPCA.B day 34 tumor was profiled by 10X Genomics Flex. After ambient-RNA removal and doublet filtering 20,598 cells remained, including 12,429 inferCNV-confirmed tumor cells. Tumor cells were scored with mouse orthologues of the polarization signature. De novo NMF programs were compared with human NMF factors by loading correlation with permutation null. KRT7 (clone: EPR17078) immunohistochemistry was performed on day 26 tumors. Briefly, FFPE sections were deparaffinized in xylene followed by tissue rehydration in decreasing levels of ethanol. Sections were rinsed twice in PBS and were subject to citrate-based heat induced antigen retrieval for 10 minutes followed by 10 minutes of tris-based retrieval. Slides were cooled, washed with PBS and treated with 3% hydrogen peroxide for 15 minutes. Slides were subsequently blocked with 2.5% horse serum for 30 minutes prior to overnight incubation with KRT7 (1:200). Slides were washed three times with PBS, incubated with rabbit secondary for 30 minutes. Slides were washed, incubated with 3,3-diaminobenzidine (DAB) for 90 seconds and counterstained with hematoxylin. Slides were dehydrated with increasing levels of ethanol, mounted with coverslips and scanned (Zeiss Z1; 20x, 0.22µm per pixel); images were exported using QuPath.

Xenium. We designed a custom 477-gene Xenium panel (v1 chemistry, Table S7). Probes were benchmarked against the atlas and 28 discordant genes were excluded from use in annotation. Cells were retained with 10 or more transcripts, 5 or more genes and an area of 10 - 500µm2 and <5% control-probe counts. TMA cores were de-arrayed, QC filtered and pooled per patient, and patients with 500 or more cells were retained for spatial and survival analyses. The final data comprise 1.9 million cells from 8 whole-tissue sections, 1.5 million TMA core cells from 503 cores, representing 378 patients and 34,281 fallopian tube epithelium cells from 15 patients. Cells were annotated automatically using SingleR using the atlas as the reference dataset. Secretory cells were split into SecA, Intermediate and SecB, resulting in 18 final cell types. Pathway modules were scored throughout using UCell.

Spatial statistics. SecA-SecB spatial association was quantified by global bivariate Moran’s I, between each secretory cell’s SecA score and the SecB scores of secretory cells within 50 µm. Weights were binary with 999 permutations per tissue and 199 per TMA core (minimum of 500 secretory cells). Per cell, it was quantified by bivariate LISA (499 permutations, BH within tissue). From cells of interest, we derived local measures of density, neighborhood pathway scores, local epithelial hypoxia or polarization scores and distance to the nearest pericyte or endothelial cell. Gradients were fitted with tissue-weighted GAMs (mgcv, s(x, k = 10) over all cells of the eight whole tissues, and immune composition with per-tissue binomial GAMs. Curves span the 1st–99th percentiles. Each panel was tested per tissue by comparing the top and bottom 20% (paired Wilcoxon, n = 8). Nuclear and cell areas are derived from Xenium segmentation. Macrophage morphology was determined in tissues or TMA patients with a minimum of 10 macrophages per tertile of the lowest and highest niche polarization. Local cell density was the number of cells within 50 µm of each secretory cell per mm² of the 50-µm circle (median per sample and state).

Visium HD. WT01 was profiled by Visium HD and analyzed in 16 and 8 µm bins. Bins were classified as epithelial or macrophage by marker UMI counts, and bin polarization was the mean z-score of the SecB minus the SecA genes. Macrophage bins with 2 or more SecB high epithelial bins within 48 µm were compared to distal macrophage bins. Fold changes were adjusted for macrophage content and genes attributed to adjacent epithelium were excluded.

Macrophage niches. In Xenium, SecB-niche macrophages had 5 or more SecB cells within 50 µm, controls had no SecB cells and a minimum of 5 SecA cells. They were compared per tissue. SecB cells within 30µm of niche macrophages were compared to SecB cells with no surrounding macrophages. For each macrophage with ≥3 secretory neighbors within 50 µm, the SecB share of those neighbors was compared between the top (hypoxic–glycolytic) and bottom (tissue-resident) tertiles of a program score. The score was nine hypoxia–glycolysis genes minus four resident genes (Table S9). The comparison was made per whole tissue and per TMA patient (n = 311).

Protein correlation. Previously published immunofluorescence intensities from TMA A were correlated per core (Pearson and Spearman; 177 final TMA A cores from 95 patients, 157–163 with IF for each marker) with Xenium transcript expression and mean polarization.

Survival. TMA survival analyses included patients with primary, pre-treatment HGSC and represented by two tumor cores. Patients given neoadjuvant chemotherapy (n = 5) or with non-HGSC histology on central review (n = 4) were excluded. Follow-up was censored at 5 years, and stage, residual disease and age had to be complete (OS n = 104, 40 events; PFS n = 103, 71 events). Kaplan–Meier curves compared patients in the lowest and highest tertiles of per-patient polarization, the middle tertile left out (log-rank test). SecA proportion, SecB proportion and mean polarization were z-scored and each tested in a Cox model adjusted for stage, residual disease and age, with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR across these six tests (Table S11). Proportional hazards were assessed with Schoenfeld residuals (Table S11). TCGA-OV polarization was compared between the highest and lowest tertiles by log-rank test and tested in Cox models adjusted for epithelial fraction (BayesPrism), stage and age. In ICON7 (GSE140082, stage III/IV, n = 191), tumors were split at the median polarization. The bevacizumab effect on PFS was estimated per group, with a 15-month time split. The treatment x polarization interaction was tested by likelihood-ratio test in a Cox model adjusted for adjusted for FIGO stage, debulking status and age. In each pair of forest plots, q is the Benjamini–Hochberg FDR across the estimates shown.

Inference used independent units: patients or samples (atlas level conclusions), models (PDOs), sections or TMA patients (Xenium) and patients (survival). Cell- and bin- level analyses are descriptive. Paired comparisons used two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Other tests were Kruskal–Wallis tests, DESeq2 Wald and limma-voom moderated t-tests on pseudobulks, permutation tests, Pearson and Spearman correlations, log-rank tests and Cox regression; all tests were two-sided. Benjamini–Hochberg FDR was applied within stated families (genes in each differential-expression analysis, BiLISA cells within each tissue, the KPCA.B loading correlations of Figure S10, and the Cox model sets of Figure 7 and Tables S11–S12); other p values are nominal. Specific test, sample n value and error definitions are defined within figure legends. Analyses used R 4.4.3 (Bioconductor 3.20) and Python 3.12.9; package versions are specified within the repository.

abstract: High-grade serous ovarian carcinoma (HGSC) is among the most genomically unstable cancers, yet how this diversity relates to malignant-cell states and how they influence treatment response remain unclear. Integrating 1.98 million single-cell transcriptomes across 13 studies, we identify a dominant axis of polarization in malignant secretory cells, from proliferative, progenitor-like (SecA) to quiescent, injury-like (SecB) states that recur across patients and coexist within genetic clones. Spatial profiling of eight whole tumors and tissue microarrays from 378 patients links this polarization to tumor architecture: SecB cells occupy avascular, hypoxic niches, where they adopt HIF/NF-κB survival programs, exclude lymphocytes, and co-organize with macrophages exhibiting similar glycolytic states. Their localization and enrichment in ascites link SecB to metastasis. SecB predicts poor survival across independent cohorts, but preferential benefit from bevacizumab in the ICON7 trial. Together, these findings reveal shared malignant phenotypes across genomically diverse tumors and highlight their potential to guide treatment selection.
